Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two nouns
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In addition to + -ing), mid-sentence blank ending in a colon; plain noun key against E, W and P rewrites
items.passage: Native to California’s Sierra Nevada, giant sequoias can survive for more than 3,000 years. In addition to growing as tall as a 25-story building, ______ bark up to 60 centimeters thick that insulates their living tissue from wildfire, and heartwood rich in tannins, chemical compounds that discourage decay and destructive insects.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: there are two traits that help giant sequoias survive for thousands of years:
two traits help giant sequoias survive for thousands of years:
giant sequoias have two traits that let them survive for thousands of years:
giant sequoias’ survival for thousands of years depends on two traits:
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. Choice C places “giant sequoias” immediately after the modifying phrase “In addition to growing as tall as a 25-story building,” making clear that the sequoias, and not another noun in the sentence, are what grow that tall.

A.why_wrong: The function word “there” follows the modifying phrase, which leaves the phrase with no noun it can logically describe.

B.why_wrong: “Two traits” follows the modifying phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the traits grow as tall as a 25-story building.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “giant sequoias’ survival,” so the sentence illogically says that the trees’ survival grows as tall as a 25-story building.

items.notes: Subject: giant sequoia bark and heartwood (natural science). Band-7 moves, after 37e5c794 (3.16): mid-sentence blank closed by a colon, so every option must also read into the list that follows; all four options carry the same content words and differ only in what lands first (E, W, P); the tempting W option is the shortest and reads as a natural topic sentence. Key is the plain noun and not the longest option.

band7.why: Same frame as the one band-7 prep_gerund official 37e5c794: mid-sentence blank closed by a colon with 25 run words after it, every option a grammatical clause carrying the same facts, E, W and P foils; D opens with “giant sequoias’” so form does not point to the key. Weakest point: the cue sits in the opener and the right subject is the plain noun, so the margin over band 6 is thin.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener describing the evidence (Drawn from recordings ...), passage-final blank; the right subject is “the findings of a 2005 study,” not the birds
items.passage: Black-capped chickadees respond to a stationary hawk or owl by mobbing it, calling loudly to recruit other songbirds into harassing the predator until it departs. Their characteristic call, the “chick-a-dee” for which the species is named, turns out to encode remarkably detailed information. Drawn from recordings of chickadees reacting to more than a dozen species of captive predators, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the birds, a 2005 study found, add more “dee” notes to the call when the predator is small and maneuverable.
biologists concluded in a 2005 study that the birds add more “dee” notes to the call when the predator is small and maneuverable.
it was shown in a 2005 study by biologists that the birds add more “dee” notes to the call when the predator is small and maneuverable.
the findings of a 2005 study showed that the birds add more “dee” notes to the call when the predator is small and maneuverable.
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. Choice D makes “the findings of a 2005 study” the subject and places it immediately after the modifying phrase “Drawn from recordings ... predators,” making clear that the findings, and not another noun in the sentence, were drawn from the recordings.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W), obvious noun with an interrupter
A.why_wrong: “The birds” follows the modifying phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the chickadees themselves were drawn from recordings.

B.why_wrong: “Biologists” follows the modifying phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the biologists were drawn from recordings.

C.why_wrong: The it-construction “it was shown” follows the modifying phrase, which leaves the phrase with no noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: black-capped chickadee alarm calls encode predator size (2005 study; no names used) (natural science). Band-7 moves, after 8b017d4e (3.27): opener about the evidence, so the right subject is a “findings of” phrase built off the obvious noun; distractor A starts with the obvious noun and carries an interrupter, as 8b017d4e’s A does; passage-final blank with a long run. Key not the longest option.

band7.why: The 8b017d4e pattern: an evidence opener (“Drawn from recordings”) makes the right subject a “findings of” phrase, while A starts with the obvious noun (the birds) and keeps every fact with an interrupter, as the model’s A does; B and C (agent, expletive) are grammatical clauses. Key noun absent from the passage.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final blank; the animals are the right subject
items.passage: Alpine swifts breed on cliffs and tall buildings in southern Europe and spend the nonbreeding season in West Africa. Biologists had long suspected that the birds rarely land outside the breeding season, but confirming this required tracking individual birds continuously for months. Carrying lightweight data loggers that weighed little more than a gram, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: three swifts tagged by researchers in Switzerland stayed airborne for more than 200 consecutive days, a 2013 study revealed.
a 2013 study revealed that three swifts tagged by researchers in Switzerland stayed airborne for more than 200 consecutive days.
the researchers’ discovery was that three swifts tagged in Switzerland had stayed airborne for more than 200 consecutive days.
more than 200 consecutive days were spent airborne by three swifts that researchers had tagged in Switzerland, a 2013 study revealed.
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. Choice A places “three swifts tagged by researchers in Switzerland” immediately after the modifying phrase “Carrying lightweight ... gram,” making clear that the swifts, and not another noun in the sentence, carried the loggers.

B.why_wrong: “A 2013 study” follows the modifying phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the study carried the data loggers.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the researchers’ discovery,” so the sentence illogically says that a discovery carried the data loggers.

D.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
D.why_wrong: “More than 200 consecutive days” follows the modifying phrase, so the sentence illogically says that a span of days carried the data loggers.

items.notes: Subject: alpine swifts staying aloft for more than 200 days (2013 tracking study; no names used) (natural science). Band 6 as 9df6da04 (3.14) and dab8b8ee (3.5): plain agent key with a trailing attribution like 3.5’s key; foils W, P and V, each keeping every fact.

fixes: explanation: quoted opener now matches the passage (“Carrying lightweight ... gram,”)

band7.why: Target 6. Plain agent key (the tagged swifts) with a trailing attribution as in dab8b8ee (3.5); W, P and passive foils each keep every fact. R3_ing_participle plain-agent items sit at band 6 in the officials.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner: plural antecedent (the birds) with the singular fish (“it”) right before the blank
items.passage: Shoebills, towering gray birds of the papyrus swamps of East and Central Africa, are patient ambush predators, standing motionless in shallow water until an unsuspecting lungfish surfaces within reach. Then the birds lunge forward and collapse onto the fish, seizing it with ______ massive, clog-shaped bills along with a mouthful of vegetation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of possessive determiners. The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees in number with the plural noun “the birds” and thus indicates that the massive bills belong to the shoebills.

A.recipe: wrong-number determiner matching the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The singular possessive determiner “its” doesn’t agree in number with the plural noun “the birds”; the bills belong to the shoebills, not to the fish.

C.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction for “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction for “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: shoebills ambushing lungfish (natural science). Band 6 as 3bceeb93 (3.4) and 2cb1ee22: antecedent “the birds” 10 words before the blank, with the singular fish (“it”) immediately before it, so the wrong-number determiner is the real foil.

band7.why: Target 6. Antecedent “the birds” 10 words back with the singular fish (“it”) right before the blank, as in the band-6 officials 3bceeb93 and 2cb1ee22; the antecedent precedes the pronoun and is under 15 words away, so not band 7.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular possessor before a plural head (the photographer’s portraits), then an appositive with its own singular verb
items.passage: Working from a studio in New York City’s Harlem neighborhood, James Van Der Zee photographed its residents for over fifty years. The photographer’s portraits from the 1920s, a decade that is often described as the creative peak of the Harlem Renaissance, ______ a confident, prosperous community of churchgoers, athletes, musicians, and families dressed in their finest clothes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The plural verb “depict” agrees in number with the plural subject “portraits.”

A.recipe: wrong number (singular present), agrees with the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The singular verb “depicts” doesn’t agree in number with the plural subject “portraits.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “has depicted” doesn’t agree in number with the plural subject “portraits.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “is depicting” doesn’t agree in number with the plural subject “portraits.”

items.notes: Subject: James Van Der Zee’s Harlem portraits (arts). Band-7 moves, after f10b7ce4 (3.25) and 863065c7 (3.23): singular possessor “photographer’s” before the plural head; 17 intervening words holding singular nouns (decade, peak, Harlem Renaissance, plus the possessor) and a relative clause with its own singular verb “is”; plural key (half of band-7 R1 keys are plural); 14 words of the run follow the blank.

band7.why: Band-7 R1_rel_poss settings (f10b7ce4, 863065c7): plural head “portraits” behind the singular possessor “photographer’s”, an appositive holding three more singular nouns and its own singular verb “is”, plural key with three singular foils in three tenses, 14 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two mass nouns, forced by “each material”
items.passage: In 1867, French gardener Joseph Monier patented concrete flowerpots strengthened with iron mesh, an early form of the reinforced concrete now used in bridges and towers. Steel bars and the concrete around them stay bonded as the air warms and cools daily because ______ coefficients of thermal expansion are nearly identical, with each material growing by about one hundred-thousandth of its length per degree Celsius.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of possessive nouns. The singular possessive nouns “steel’s” and “concrete’s” correctly indicate that each material has its own coefficient of thermal expansion, as the phrase “with each material growing” makes clear.

A.recipe: missing apostrophes on both possessors (plain plurals)
A.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive nouns “steel’s” and “concrete’s,” not the plural nouns “steels” and “concretes.”

C.recipe: missing apostrophe on the first possessor (plain plural)
C.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “steel’s,” not the plural noun “steels.”

D.recipe: joint possession where each noun owns its own
D.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “steel’s,” not the singular noun “steel”; each material has its own coefficient, so each noun must be possessive.

items.notes: Subject: why steel and concrete work together (matched thermal expansion), with Joseph Monier’s 1867 patent as context (history of technology / engineering). Band 7 after 4c335aea (3.28): individual possession of two singular mass nouns, the four-option grid of the model, the cue for separate possession (“each material”) placed 9 words after the blank.

fixes: explanation: cue phrase quoted as in the passage (“with each material growing”, not “lengthening”)

band7.why: Mirrors the one band-7 R6_individual official 4c335aea: the same four-option grid on two singular mass nouns, and the individual-possession cue (“each material”) sits 9 words after the blank, so D (joint possession) reads correctly until then.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: absolute phrase (noun + -ing) after a complete clause; finite options make comma splices
items.passage: The villages of Shirakawa-gō, in a snowy, mountainous region of central Japan, are celebrated for their gasshō-zukuri farmhouses, a name meaning “constructed like hands in prayer.” Assembled without metal fasteners, the houses have steeply pitched thatched roofs, their sharp angle ______ accumulated snow to slide off before its weight can damage the timber framework beneath.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of verb forms within a sentence. The nonfinite present participle “allowing” correctly forms a supplementary element with “their sharp angle” that modifies the main clause “the houses have steeply pitched thatched roofs,” describing what the roofs’ pitch does.

A.recipe: finite verb after an absolute-phrase noun (comma splice)
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “has allowed” creates a second main clause, and two main clauses can’t be joined with only a comma after “roofs.”

B.recipe: finite verb after an absolute-phrase noun (comma splice)
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “allows” creates a second main clause, and two main clauses can’t be joined with only a comma after “roofs.”

D.recipe: finite verb after an absolute-phrase noun (comma splice)
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “allowed” creates a second main clause, and two main clauses can’t be joined with only a comma after “roofs.”

items.notes: Subject: gasshō-zukuri farmhouses of Shirakawa-gō (history / architecture). Band-7 moves, after 81f09e07 and c88ba1b7: absolute phrase after a complete clause; the noun before the blank (“their sharp angle”) lets every finite option form a full, sensible clause, so the error is a comma splice; the present “allows” matches the passage’s present tense and is the strongest foil.

band7.why: The 81f09e07 / c88ba1b7 absolute-phrase pattern: complete clause, comma, “their sharp angle” + blank, so every finite option (has allowed, allows, allowed) forms a full, sensible clause and fails only as a comma splice; “allows” matches the passage’s present tense. 13 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (phenomenon) followed by a relative clause with a plural subject and verb
items.passage: In a 1966 experiment, social psychologist Elliot Aronson found that students liked a nearly flawless quiz contestant more after hearing him spill coffee on himself. This phenomenon, which psychologists call the pratfall effect, ______ why audiences often warm to experts who make small, harmless mistakes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The singular verb “explains” agrees in number with the singular subject “phenomenon.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “explain” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “phenomenon.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are explaining” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “phenomenon.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have explained” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “phenomenon.”

items.notes: Subject: the pratfall effect (Aronson, Willerman and Floyd 1966) (social science). Medium: one plural noun with its own plural verb (“psychologists call”) between the head and the blank.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid, singular possessor + plain plural noun
items.passage: Ivo Andrić’s 1945 novel The Bridge on the Drina spans nearly four centuries in Višegrad, a town in eastern Bosnia. Instead of following a single hero, the novel traces the lives of the ______ from the bridge’s construction in the 1570s to its partial destruction in 1914.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of plural and possessive nouns. The singular possessive noun “town’s” indicates that the inhabitants belong to one town, Višegrad, and the plural noun “inhabitants” correctly refers to the many people whose lives the novel traces.

A.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “town’s,” not the plural noun “towns.”

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: The context requires the plural noun “inhabitants,” not the singular possessive noun “inhabitant’s.”

C.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe
C.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “town’s,” not the plural possessive “towns’,” and the plural noun “inhabitants,” not the plural possessive “inhabitants’.”

items.notes: Subject: Ivo Andrić, The Bridge on the Drina (literature). Grid built as 2.24: possessor x possessed noun, three wrong cells.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun: singular antecedent (the city) with the plural “tablets” as subject of the same clause
items.passage: Since large-scale excavations began at Hattusa in central Turkey in 1906, archaeologists have recovered some 30,000 clay tablets there. Written mostly in cuneiform, the tablets show that the city served as the capital of the Hittite Empire for centuries before ______ fell into ruin around 1200 BCE.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is pronoun-antecedent agreement. The singular pronoun “it” agrees in number with the singular antecedent “the city” (Hattusa), which is what fell into ruin.

A.recipe: wrong-number pronoun matching the nearest plural
A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “the city.”

C.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “the city.”

D.why_wrong: The pronoun “one” has no clear antecedent here; it leaves unclear what fell into ruin.

items.notes: Subject: Hattusa and its tablet archive (history). Medium: the plural “the tablets,” subject of the same sentence, competes with the singular antecedent “the city.”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject (X and Y) followed by an appositive ending in a singular noun
items.passage: In 2016, Ukrainian mathematician Maryna Viazovska and her collaborators settled a question about stacking spheres that had puzzled geometers for decades. The E8 lattice and the Leech lattice, two ways of arranging identical spheres in a higher-dimensional space, ______ the densest possible packings in eight and twenty-four dimensions, respectively.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The plural verb “are” agrees in number with the compound subject “The E8 lattice and the Leech lattice.”

A.recipe: wrong number (singular present), agrees with “the Leech lattice” or “space”
A.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree in number with the compound subject “The E8 lattice and the Leech lattice.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree in number with the compound subject “The E8 lattice and the Leech lattice.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree in number with the compound subject “The E8 lattice and the Leech lattice.”

items.notes: Subject: Maryna Viazovska and the sphere-packing problem in dimensions 8 and 24 (mathematics, science). Medium as 2.13: compound subject of two singular nouns plus an appositive whose last noun (“space”) is singular.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner: plural antecedent (moon jars) with singular nouns (the clay, the kiln) nearby
items.passage: Potters in Korea during the Joseon dynasty made large white porcelain jars by throwing two bowl-shaped halves on a wheel and joining them at the rim. Because the clay often sagged slightly in the heat of the kiln, these “moon jars” are rarely perfectly round, and collectors prize ______ gently uneven outlines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of possessive determiners. The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees in number with the plural noun “moon jars” and thus indicates that the uneven outlines belong to the jars.

B.why_wrong: The singular possessive determiner “its” doesn’t agree in number with the plural noun “moon jars.”

C.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction for “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction for “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: Joseon porcelain moon jars (arts). Medium: singular “the clay” and “the kiln” sit between the antecedent and the blank.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual action (“On mild days in late winter”)
items.passage: Snow fleas are not true fleas but springtails, tiny wingless arthropods that normally inhabit leaf litter and soil. On mild days in late winter, however, they ______ up through the snowpack by the thousands, congregating on its surface in such numbers that the snow appears sprinkled with pepper.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is verb tense. The present tense verb “climb” is consistent with the other present tense verbs in the text (“are,” “inhabit”) and correctly describes something snow fleas do regularly, on mild days in late winter.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense verb “climbed” isn’t consistent with the present tense used to describe this regular behavior.

C.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
C.why_wrong: The past perfect verb “had climbed” isn’t consistent with the present tense used to describe this regular behavior.

D.why_wrong: The future perfect verb “will have climbed” isn’t consistent with the present tense used to describe this regular behavior.

items.notes: Subject: snow fleas (springtails) emerging on snow (natural science).

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a general practice, parallel with “becomes”
items.passage: Lunfardo, an informal vocabulary that developed in Buenos Aires in the late 1800s, still appears frequently in tango lyrics and everyday conversation there. In one of its most playful variations, called vesre, speakers ______ the syllables of a word, so “café” becomes “feca” and “tango” becomes “gotán.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is verb tense. The present tense verb “reverse” is consistent with the present tense verbs “appears” and “becomes” and correctly describes a practice that is still current.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense verb “reversed” isn’t consistent with the present tense verbs “appears” and “becomes.”

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect verb “had reversed” isn’t consistent with the present tense verbs “appears” and “becomes.”

C.why_wrong: The conditional perfect “would have reversed” describes something that didn’t happen, which doesn’t fit a practice the text presents as real and current.

items.notes: Subject: Lunfardo and vesre syllable reversal in Buenos Aires (social science, linguistics).

fixes: why_wrong A and B cited a verb “colors” that is not in the passage; now “appears” and “becomes”

items.subtype: Personal pronoun: singular subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: British composer Ethel Smyth wrote “The March of the Women” as an anthem for the suffrage campaign, which sought to win women the right to vote. In 1912, while imprisoned for participating in a protest, ______ conducted fellow prisoners singing the anthem from her cell window, using a toothbrush as a baton.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is pronoun-antecedent agreement. The singular pronoun “she” agrees in number with the singular antecedent “Ethel Smyth,” the person who was imprisoned.

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “Ethel Smyth.”

C.why_wrong: The pronoun “it” doesn’t refer to a person, so it can’t refer to Ethel Smyth.

D.why_wrong: The first-person pronoun “we” doesn’t agree with the antecedent “Ethel Smyth,” who is referred to in the third person.

items.notes: Subject: Ethel Smyth conducting from her Holloway cell, 1912 (arts, music).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head (mummies) with a short participial intervener
items.passage: The Chinchorro people, who fished and gathered shellfish along the coast of the Atacama Desert, deliberately preserved their dead. Their mummies, some prepared as early as 5000 BCE, ______ approximately two thousand years older than the earliest intentionally preserved mummies of Egypt.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The plural verb “are” agrees in number with the plural subject “mummies.”

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree in number with the plural subject “mummies.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree in number with the plural subject “mummies.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree in number with the plural subject “mummies.”

items.notes: Subject: Chinchorro mummies (history, archaeology).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (the bacterium) with a short interrupter
items.passage: High doses of radiation kill most living things by shattering their DNA. The bacterium Deinococcus radiodurans, however, ______ able to survive doses about a thousand times greater than the amount that would kill a person, efficiently repairing its broken chromosomes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The singular verb “is” agrees in number with the singular subject “the bacterium Deinococcus radiodurans.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “the bacterium.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “the bacterium.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “the bacterium.”

items.notes: Subject: Deinococcus radiodurans and radiation (natural science).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (the poem), no intervener
items.passage: Argentine poet Alfonsina Storni published “Tú me quieres blanca” (“You Want Me White”) in her 1918 collection El dulce daño. The poem ______ a lover who expects absolute purity from a woman while holding himself to no comparable standard.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The singular verb “criticizes” agrees in number with the singular subject “the poem.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “criticize” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “the poem.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are criticizing” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “the poem.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have criticized” doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject “the poem.”

items.notes: Subject: Alfonsina Storni, “Tú me quieres blanca” (literature).

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a short subject
items.passage: The southern cassowary, a flightless bird that can stand nearly two meters tall, inhabits the rainforests of northeastern Australia and New Guinea. The bird ______ the fruits of more than 200 plant species, often swallowing them whole and later dispersing their seeds across the forest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of verb forms within a sentence. A main clause requires a finite verb to describe the action of the subject (in this case, “the bird”), and this choice supplies the finite present tense verb “eats.”

B.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: The nonfinite participle “eating” doesn’t supply the sentence with a finite main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

C.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The nonfinite form “having eaten” doesn’t supply the sentence with a finite main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

D.recipe: to-infinitive where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite to-infinitive “to eat” doesn’t supply the sentence with a finite main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

items.notes: Subject: southern cassowary as a seed disperser (natural science).

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid, singular possessor + plain plural noun
items.passage: Russian painter Zinaida Serebriakova completed her most celebrated work, the self-portrait At the Dressing Table, in 1909, when she was in her mid-twenties. In the painting, the ______ are arranged across a dressing table as she combs her hair in front of a mirror, her reflection gazing confidently at the viewer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of plural and possessive nouns. The singular possessive noun “artist’s” indicates that the belongings are Serebriakova’s, and the plural noun “belongings” correctly refers to more than one object on the table.

A.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “artist’s,” not the plural noun “artists.”

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: The context requires the plural noun “belongings,” not the singular possessive noun “belonging’s.”

D.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “artist’s,” not the plural possessive “artists’,” and the plural noun “belongings,” not the plural possessive “belongings’.”

items.notes: Subject: Zinaida Serebriakova, At the Dressing Table (arts).

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid, singular possessor + plain plural noun
items.passage: With its velvety brown coat and zebra-like stripes, the okapi of central Africa’s rainforests is frequently mistaken for a relative of the zebra, but it is actually the giraffe’s closest living relative. The distinctive stripes on the ______ may help a young okapi follow its mother through dense undergrowth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of plural and possessive nouns. The singular possessive noun “animal’s” indicates that the legs belong to the okapi, and the plural noun “legs” correctly refers to more than one leg.

A.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “animal’s,” not the plural noun “animals.”

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: The context requires the plural noun “legs,” not the singular possessive noun “leg’s.”

D.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “animal’s,” not the plural possessive “animals’,” and the plural noun “legs,” not the plural possessive “legs’.”

items.notes: Subject: the okapi’s striped legs (natural science).

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action completed before a dated past event (“By then”)
items.passage: In 1874, the University of Göttingen in Germany awarded Russian mathematician Sofia Kovalevskaya a doctorate, making her one of the first women in modern Europe to earn one in mathematics. By then, Kovalevskaya ______ three original papers, including one on the shape of Saturn’s rings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is verb tense. The past perfect verb “had written” correctly indicates that Kovalevskaya wrote the papers before a specific point in the past, 1874, when she was awarded her doctorate.

B.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: The present tense verb “writes” doesn’t indicate that the writing was completed before 1874.

C.why_wrong: The future perfect verb “will have written” doesn’t indicate that the writing was completed before 1874.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive verb “is writing” doesn’t indicate that the writing was completed before 1874.

items.notes: Subject: Sofia Kovalevskaya’s 1874 Göttingen doctorate (history of mathematics).

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate (gave ... and played)
items.passage: Venezuelan pianist and composer Teresa Carreño was a remarkable child prodigy. She gave her first public concert in New York City in 1862, at the age of eight, and ______ for President Abraham Lincoln at the White House the following year, a performance that further established her reputation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is the use of verb forms within a sentence. The finite past tense verb “played” is parallel with the finite verb “gave” and correctly completes the compound predicate whose subject is “She.”

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The nonfinite participle “playing” can’t join “gave” as the second verb of the compound predicate; a finite verb is needed.

B.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: The nonfinite form “having played” can’t join “gave” as the second verb of the compound predicate; a finite verb is needed.

C.recipe: to-infinitive where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The to-infinitive “to play” can’t join “gave” as the second verb of the compound predicate; a finite verb is needed.

items.notes: Subject: Teresa Carreño, child pianist who played for Lincoln (arts, music).

fixes: passage: summative appositive “an invitation” renamed playing at the White House, which is not an invitation; now “a performance”

items.subtype: Tense: simple past with a stated year
items.passage: Chinese writer Ding Ling achieved literary fame in her early twenties with a single, groundbreaking short story. In 1928, she ______ “Miss Sophia’s Diary,” an unusually candid account, told through diary entries, of a young woman’s restless emotional life in Beijing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The convention being tested is verb tense. The simple past tense verb “published” is consistent with the reference to a specific time in the past, 1928.

A.recipe: present simple where past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present tense verb “publishes” isn’t consistent with the past year 1928.

B.why_wrong: The future tense verb “will publish” isn’t consistent with the past year 1928.

D.recipe: present perfect next to a dated past
D.why_wrong: The present perfect verb “has published” isn’t used with a specific past time such as 1928.

items.notes: Subject: Ding Ling, “Miss Sophia’s Diary” (literature).
